23823: If the result is fixed, preaching is pointless theatre; if it is not, election means nothing.
23824: Historically, many of the most active missionaries (William Carey, George Whitefield, Charles Spurgeon) held strong views of election and saw no contradiction, because they believed God works through means. Arminians reach the same urgency by a different route. Whatever one thinks of each system, both lead to mission in practice.
23825: Christians share their faith with confidence that results rest with God and with seriousness that their witness matters. Election, rightly held, removes both pride when people respond and despair when they do not.
23826: Kept secure, yet warned against falling away
23827: Jesus says no one will snatch his sheep from his hand, and Paul says nothing can separate believers from God's love. Yet Hebrews warns that those who have tasted the heavenly gift and fall away cannot be restored, and Paul tells believers to continue in the faith if they are to be presented holy.
23828: Scripture gives believers deep assurance and serious warnings, and traditions explain how both function differently.
23830: No one will snatch them out of my hand. Nothing can separate us from the love of God. He who began a good work will complete it. You are guarded by God's power.
23832: It is impossible to restore those who have tasted the heavenly gift and then fallen away. If we go on sinning deliberately, no sacrifice remains. You will be presented holy, if you continue in the faith.
23833: If true believers cannot be lost, why warn them? If they can be lost, how can they be assured?
23834: Perseverance of the saints: warnings are means
23835: Reformed theology, e.g. John Calvin, Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday (*The Race Set Before Us*)
23836: True believers will persevere, and God uses the warnings as one of the means by which they persevere, like a sign at a cliff edge that keeps a driver on the road. Those who finally fall away show they never truly belonged.
23838: Arminian, Wesleyan, many Pentecostal and Holiness churches; Catholic and Orthodox in their own terms
23839: Believers are secure in Christ as long as they remain in him by faith. No outside power can snatch them, but they can freely walk away. The warnings describe a real danger for real believers, and assurance rests on present trust, not a past decision.
23841: Some Baptists and dispensationalists, e.g. Zane Hodges, Charles Ryrie in a moderate form
23842: Anyone who has truly believed is eternally secure even if they later stop believing. The warnings concern loss of rewards, discipline or fruitfulness, not loss of salvation. Critics say this undercuts holiness; defenders say it alone preserves grace as unconditional.
23845: Hebrews 6 describes what would happen if a believer could fall away, to show how serious apostasy is, while the writer is confident of 'better things' for his readers. Critics regard this as weakening a real warning.
23846: Each side simply ignores the other half of the texts. The Bible doesn't have a consistent position.
23847: Each tradition offers an account of both sets of texts, not just one. Hebrews itself combines the strongest warning with 'we are confident of better things in your case', which suggests the writer saw both as working together. Whether one tradition's account is better is a fair debate.
23848: Believers can rest in God's keeping while taking spiritual drift seriously. Pastorally, assurance is offered to the anxious and warnings to the complacent.
23849: Grace is free, yet discipleship costs everything
23850: Isaiah invites people to come and buy without money and without price, and Revelation ends with 'take the water of life without price'. Jesus says whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be his disciple.
23851: Grace cannot be bought, but receiving it means giving one's whole life to the giver.
23853: Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. The free gift of God is eternal life. Justified freely by his grace. Let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
23855: Any of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. Count the cost. Take up your cross daily. The kingdom is like a man who sells everything to buy a field.
23856: If grace is free, why does Jesus demand everything? If it costs everything, how is it free?
23858: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (*The Cost of Discipleship*), and widely adopted across traditions
23859: Bonhoeffer called forgiveness without repentance or discipleship 'cheap grace'. Real grace is free because nothing we pay earns it, and costly because it cost God his Son and because it calls us to follow. The cost is not the price of grace but the shape of a life that has received it.
23861: John MacArthur and many Reformed evangelicals
23862: Saving faith includes submission to Jesus as Lord. One cannot receive him as Saviour while refusing him as Lord. This is not works earning salvation, but the nature of the faith that saves.
23863: Free Grace: salvation free, discipleship a second step
23864: Zane Hodges, Charles Ryrie and the Free Grace movement
23865: Eternal life is received by believing alone; the costly demands of Luke 14 describe discipleship, a further commitment open to believers. This keeps grace entirely free; critics say it splits what Jesus joins.
23867: Many interpreters, from patristic to modern
23868: In Jesus' parable, the man sells everything 'in his joy'. The cost is not felt as a fee but as the obvious response to something far more valuable. Free and costly meet in the experience of finding something worth more than everything.
23869: Calling something free and then demanding everything is a bait-and-switch.
23870: Jesus does the opposite of hiding the cost: in Luke 14 he tells crowds to sit down and count it before following. The offer is free in that no one can pay for it, and the cost is stated openly as what following involves. Many relationships, such as marriage, work like this: love is given, not bought, but receiving it reorders a whole life.
23871: Christians are freed from trying to earn God's favour and called to hold nothing back from him. The paradox guards against both legalism and casual, cost-free religion.
23872: The law abolished, yet not abolished but fulfilled
23873: Ephesians says Christ abolished the law of commandments in his flesh. In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it, and not one dot will pass away. Christians have argued about which parts of the Old Testament law still apply ever since.
23874: Christ ends the law as a dividing wall and a covenant, while fulfilling and carrying forward its deepest purpose.
23876: He abolished the law of commandments and ordinances. Christ is the end of the law. We are no longer under a guardian. The first covenant is obsolete.
23878: I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them. Not an iota will pass from the law until all is accomplished. Do we overthrow the law by faith? By no means; we uphold it.
23879: Jesus says he did not abolish the law; Ephesians says he did. Should Christians keep the Old Testament law or not?
23881: Thomas Aquinas, John Calvin, the Westminster Confession (ch. 19), much Reformed and Catholic teaching
23882: The law has moral, ceremonial and civil parts. Ceremonial laws (sacrifices, purity) are fulfilled and ended in Christ; Israel's civil laws ended with Israel's national covenant; moral law (summed up in the Ten Commandments) still binds. Critics note that the Bible does not label laws this way; defenders say the categories are implied by the New Testament's own handling.
23883: New Covenant Theology and Lutheran law-gospel
23884: New Covenant Theology (e.g. Tom Schreiner, Douglas Moo), Lutheran theology, many dispensationalists
23885: The whole Mosaic covenant has ended as a covenant; Christians are under 'the law of Christ'. Old Testament laws apply only as they are taken up in Christ's teaching and the apostles'. 'Fulfil' means Jesus brings the law to its goal, which changes its role.
23887: Messianic Jewish theology (in varied forms), some Hebrew Roots groups, and some scholars of the 'Paul within Judaism' school
23888: Jesus and the first Jewish believers kept the Torah, and Ephesians refers to the wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile, not to the commandments as such. Jewish believers may continue Torah observance as covenant faithfulness, while Gentiles are not required to (Acts 15). Critics say this divides the church; defenders say it respects Israel's calling.
23890: Many New Testament scholars across traditions
23891: Jesus fulfils the law as a destination fulfils a road: everything it pointed to, such as sacrifice, priesthood and temple, is realized in him. Once fulfilled, the pointers change role. Both Matthew and Ephesians are then speaking of one event from different angles.
23892: Christians pick and choose which laws to keep, enforcing some and ignoring others with no consistent principle.
23893: Christians do disagree, and some applications have been inconsistent. But every major tradition has an explicit principle for which laws continue and why, drawn from the New Testament, which already sets aside food laws and circumcision for Gentile believers while affirming love of neighbour. The charge is fair as a challenge to apply one's principle consistently.
23894: Christians read the Old Testament law as God's word that reveals his character and points to Christ, without making Mosaic ritual the way to belong to God. The love commands remain the heart of it.
23895: Texts that sound like all will be saved, and texts of final judgement
23896: Some verses say in Christ all will be made alive, God will reconcile all things, and every knee will bow and tongue confess. Others speak of eternal punishment, a narrow way that few find, and a second death. Readers have taken these texts in very different directions.
23897: Scripture holds out a cosmic hope and a serious judgement; Christians disagree about how far that hope reaches.
23899: As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. Through him God reconciles all things. Every knee will bow and every tongue confess Jesus is Lord. God has consigned all to disobedience that he may have mercy on all.
23901: They will go away into eternal punishment. Narrow is the way and few find it. They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction. Whoever was not found in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.
23902: If 'all' means everyone, how can some face eternal punishment? If some face eternal punishment, what do the 'all' texts mean?
23903: Majority position in Catholic, Orthodox (in its own nuances) and Protestant history; Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, Jonathan Edwards
23904: The 'all' texts refer to all kinds of people, all who are in Christ, or every being's acknowledgement of Christ's lordship, willing or not. Judgement texts describe a final, everlasting separation. Matthew 25:46 uses the same word 'eternal' for life and punishment.
23905: John Stott (tentatively), Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock, Seventh-day Adventists, and a growing number of evangelicals
23906: Immortality is God's gift to the saved. The unrepentant are finally destroyed, which is eternal in its result. Then God will be 'all in all' with no rebellion left, which also accounts for the 'all things reconciled' texts.
23908: Origen (as commonly understood), Gregory of Nyssa, George MacDonald, and modern writers such as Thomas Talbott and David Bentley Hart
23909: Judgement is real and may be long and severe, but it is corrective, and in the end all will be reconciled to God. The Greek 'aionios' can mean 'of the age to come' rather than endless. 'All' means all, and God's love does not finally fail.
23910: Hans Urs von Balthasar, Karl Barth (as often read), and some contemporary theologians
23911: We cannot say all will be saved, but we may pray and hope that hell is finally empty. Both sets of texts are left standing without forcing a conclusion either way.
23912: The Bible is simply inconsistent about final destiny; different authors had different beliefs.
23913: Some scholars do read the New Testament as containing diverse eschatologies. But the strongest 'all' texts and strong judgement texts often appear in the same author: Paul writes both 1 Corinthians 15:22 and 2 Thessalonians 1:9. That suggests at least the authors themselves did not see them as contradictory, though how they fit is genuinely debated.
23914: All views take sin and judgement seriously and hope in God's justice and mercy. The disagreement affects how people preach, how urgently they evangelize, and how they grieve for those who die without faith.
23915: God wants all to be saved, yet not all are saved
23916: Paul says God desires all people to be saved, and Peter says God is not willing that any should perish. Ezekiel says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. Yet scripture also says many walk the broad road to destruction.
23917: If God wills all to be saved and not all are, then either God's will has layers or people can resist it; traditions choose different explanations.
23919: God desires all people to be saved. He is not willing that any should perish but that all should reach repentance. I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. How often I would have gathered your children.
23921: Wide is the gate that leads to destruction, and many enter it. Many are called but few are chosen. You refuse to come to me that you may have life.
23922: If an all-powerful God wants all to be saved, why are some lost? Either God does not really want it, or he cannot achieve what he wants.
23924: Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox traditions; C. S. Lewis (*The Great Divorce*)
23925: God truly desires everyone's salvation but will not force love. He gives grace to all, and some refuse. The 'doors of hell are locked from the inside'. Jesus' lament over Jerusalem shows God's will being resisted by people's 'you were not willing'.
23927: Reformed theology, e.g. John Calvin, John Piper ('Are There Two Wills in God?')
23928: God's revealed will (what he commands and delights in) is that all repent; his decretive will (what he ordains to happen) includes that not all are saved, for reasons of his own glory and justice. God can truly lament a thing he permits for a greater purpose, as a judge can grieve the sentence he passes.
23930: Some Reformed interpreters (e.g. John Owen on 2 Peter 3:9)
23931: In 1 Timothy 2 'all people' is linked to prayer for kings and those in authority, meaning all kinds of people, not every individual. 2 Peter 3:9 may refer to 'you', the believing readers. Critics find this narrowing unconvincing in Ezekiel 18 and 33.
23932: God's desire will finally be fulfilled
23933: Christian universalists (see the related paradox), e.g. Thomas Talbott
23934: God's desire that all be saved will not ultimately fail; 'not all are saved' describes the present or the age to come, not the final end. Critics say this does not do justice to the finality of judgement texts.
23935: A God who wants everyone saved but lets many be lost is either weak or insincere.
23936: Each Christian answer meets this differently: free-will views say a world with real love requires the possibility of refusal; Reformed views say God has a purpose behind permitting what he does not delight in; universalists say God's desire will be met. The objection presses each view hard, which is why the debate continues, but each has a coherent account.
23937: Christians pray for everyone, including rulers, because God desires all to be saved. It grounds the conviction that no one is beyond God's love or prayer.
23938: Freely forgiven, yet forgiven only if we forgive
23939: The New Testament says forgiveness is a free gift through Christ's blood. Yet Jesus says that if you do not forgive others, your Father will not forgive you. The parable of the unforgiving servant ends with a forgiven man thrown into prison for refusing to forgive.
23940: God's forgiveness is not earned by forgiving others, but a heart that refuses to forgive shows it has not truly received God's forgiveness.
23942: In him we have forgiveness according to the riches of his grace. While we were still sinners Christ died for us. If we confess, he is faithful to forgive.
23944: If you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Judgement is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy.
23945: If forgiveness is a gift, how can it depend on our forgiving others? Doesn't that make our forgiveness a work that earns God's?
23946: Forgiving as evidence of being forgiven
23948: In the parable of the unforgiving servant the master forgives first, freely. The servant's refusal to forgive shows he has not grasped or received that mercy. Forgiving others is not the price of forgiveness but its natural overflow, and its absence reveals a heart closed to grace.
23950: Catholic and Orthodox teaching; many Wesleyan writers
23951: Forgiveness is not only a once-for-all verdict but an ongoing relationship. A person who hardens their heart against others closes themselves to God's continuing mercy, and can lose what they were given, as the parable shows. Hence the daily prayer 'forgive us as we forgive'.
23954: Some read Matthew 6:15 as about fellowship and discipline among believers, not eternal salvation: an unforgiving believer forfeits close fellowship with the Father. Critics say this softens Jesus' direct warning.
23955: So Christian forgiveness is conditional after all. Grace is free only until you fail to forgive someone.
23956: The texts present a condition, but not a payment: one does not earn mercy by forgiving, any more than a person earns a gift by opening their hands. The point of the parable is that mercy received and mercy refused cannot coexist in the same heart. Different traditions disagree about whether failure here forfeits salvation or reveals its absence.
23957: Christians are taught to forgive not as a way to earn God's favour but as a response to it, and to see bitterness as spiritually dangerous. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong did not happen or removing every consequence.
23958: Lose your life to find it
23959: Jesus says that people who try to hang on to their lives will lose them, and people who let go of their lives for his sake will find them. It sounds like nonsense if 'life' means the same thing both times. The saying works because it plays on two meanings of life: the self we grip and protect, and the deeper life God gives.
23960: The life you grip shrinks; the life you hand over to God comes back larger.
23962: Following Jesus means denying yourself, taking up a cross and being willing to lose your life.
23964: The one who loses life for Jesus' sake will find it, keep it and gain eternal life; Jesus came so people would have life abundantly.
23965: If the goal is life, why is the path loss? And if loss is the path, is Christianity simply a call to self-hatred? The saying seems to make the same thing both the price and the prize.
23967: The Greek word *psyche* can mean physical life, the self, or the whole person. Jesus contrasts the self-protective life (security, status, comfort as the final goal) with the life that comes from God. Holding the first as ultimate costs you the second.
23969: Early church readers, many Catholic and Orthodox writers, and scholars focused on the original setting
23970: In the first setting the cross was literal: some disciples would actually die. The promise is that death for Christ is not the end, because God raises the dead. The saying is first about physical death and future resurrection, and only then about everyday self-denial.
23972: Monastic, Pietist, Wesleyan and many evangelical devotional traditions
23973: Luke adds 'daily': the cross is a habit of putting God and neighbour ahead of self-will. The 'finding' is experienced now as freedom from the anxious project of self-protection, not only after death.
23975: Johannine readers; Augustine and many preachers
23976: John frames it with a grain of wheat: it must fall into the ground and die to bear fruit. The loss is real but it is the loss of a seed, not of a stone. The pattern is first Jesus' own death and resurrection, then the disciple's.
23977: This is a manipulative contradiction: it tells people to give up their lives and calls that gaining them, which can be used to justify abuse, burnout or needless martyrdom.
23978: The saying is a paradox, not a contradiction, because 'life' is used in two senses. It is also qualified: the loss is 'for my sake and the gospel's', not for any leader's convenience. The same Jesus warns against loading burdens on others and rebukes leaders who lord it over people. Christians have sometimes misused the text, but the text itself sets love of God and neighbour, not self-destruction, as the goal.
23979: Ask where you are gripping: reputation, money, control, safety. Letting go there is not losing yourself but making room for God. It does not mean neglecting your health or accepting mistreatment; Jesus withdrew to rest and avoided danger when his time had not come (Mark 6:31, John 7:1).
23981: Paul asked God three times to take away a painful 'thorn in the flesh'. God said no, telling him that grace was enough and that divine power is made perfect in weakness. So Paul says, 'when I am weak, then I am strong'.
23982: Weakness is not the opposite of God's power; it is often where that power shows most clearly.
23984: Paul is genuinely weak: afflicted, insulted, in hardships and distress, carrying treasure in a clay jar.
23986: In that very weakness Christ's power rests on him, so that he can say he is strong.
23987: Strength and weakness seem to exclude each other. If God is powerful, why not simply remove the weakness? And does praising weakness make Christianity passive or resigned?
23989: Reformed and Lutheran theology (Luther's 'theology of the cross')
23990: Human weakness removes the illusion that results come from our ability. When strength remains obviously God's, God gets the credit and we stop trusting ourselves. The clay jar shows that the power belongs to God.
23992: Many New Testament scholars (e.g. those stressing 'cruciformity') and Catholic and Orthodox spirituality
23993: Jesus was 'crucified in weakness' yet lives by God's power. The apostle shares that pattern. Weakness is not a malfunction but the shape of Christ's own path from cross to resurrection.
23996: The promise is not that weakness disappears but that grace is enough for each moment. The strength is endurance, courage and fruitfulness inside the limits, not escape from them.
23999: Paul is answering rival 'super-apostles' who boasted of impressive gifts and presence. By boasting in weakness he redefines what counts as apostolic credentials. The paradox is partly rhetoric aimed at a specific church dispute, though it states a lasting principle.
24000: Saying weakness is strength is a way of explaining away unanswered prayer: if God helps, he is strong; if he doesn't, weakness is 'strength'. The claim can't lose.
24001: Paul admits the prayer was refused and the pain stayed. He does not deny weakness; he claims something else happened through it: endurance and effective ministry that he attributes to God. Whether one accepts that attribution is a matter of faith, but the claim is not empty: Paul lists concrete sufferings and concrete outcomes. Christians also pray for healing elsewhere in the New Testament (Jas 5:14-15), so the text does not teach that God never removes weakness.
24002: Name a limitation honestly instead of hiding it. Pray for it to be removed, as Paul did, and also ask what God might do through it if it stays. Communities can learn to value people whose weakness is visible rather than only the polished and gifted.
